known_bugs_context.FP-SUB08: feeOnTop not signed in EIP-712 (REJECTED — cosigner controls executor, intentional design)

hypotheses.title: afterSwapRefund reentrancy via WETH→ETH callback enables CLOB order-book manipulation
hypotheses.mechanism: afterSwapRefund (L315) lacks the nonReentrant modifier present on ammHandleTransfer (L229), withdrawToken (L392), openOrder (L482), and closeOrder (L433). When tokenOut is WRAPPED_NATIVE, afterSwapRefund calls IWrappedNativeExtended.withdrawToAccount(executor, refundAmount) at L322, which sends ETH to the executor's address. If the executor is a contract, its receive() function fires BEFORE afterSwapRefund returns. At this point: (1) the swap settlement is 100% complete (amountOut already sent to recipient at L2237, maker balances already credited at L2234 CLOBHelper), (2) the AMM's reentrancy guard is unlocked because _finalizeSwapCollectFundsAndDisburse has returned, and (3) CLOBTransferHandler's reentrancy guard is also unlocked because ammHandleTransfer has returned. The executor's receive() can therefore call CLOBTransferHandler.openOrder() with a price below the just-exhausted currentPrice, forcing CLOBHelper.openOrder (L118-120) to reset currentPrice. This does not directly steal funds in the same transaction, but enables a sandwich: place low-price order before the swap, allow swap to exhaust order book, ETH callback resurrects currentPrice to the new low order, subsequent fills execute at the sandwiched price.
hypotheses.attack_scenario: 1. Attacker deploys MaliciousExecutor contract with a manipulative receive(). 2. Attacker opens a CLOB order at price P_low (below market). 3. Victim submits swap that exhausts order book up to P_high. 4. afterSwapRefund sends ETH refund to MaliciousExecutor.receive(). 5. In receive(), attacker calls openOrder at P_low again, resetting currentPrice to P_low. 6. In a subsequent tx (same block), attacker fills the revived P_low order profitably.
hypotheses.settlement_conservation_impact: No direct single-tx conservation violation. Enables inter-tx price manipulation that extracts value from future swappers.
references: Guardian H-01 (missing hook in CLOB, ACKNOWLEDGED) — related but distinct mechanism

hypotheses.title: CLOBHelper.fillOrder reads storage slot 0 for endingOrderNonce when order book exhausted
hypotheses.mechanism: When traverseCLOB exhausts the order book (nextOrderId == bytes32(0)), it calls _orderIdToOrder(bytes32(0)) at L289, which sets the storage pointer to slot 0 via inline assembly. The Order struct at slot 0 is: maker = address(0), orderNonce = value at slot 0 words 1+ (unrelated contract state). fillOrder then assigns endingOrderNonce = ptrOrder.orderNonce at L237, reading whatever happens to live at storage slot 0 of CLOBTransferHandler. The CLOBTransferHandler stores _status (ReentrancyGuard) at slot 0. After a nonReentrant call, _status = 1 (NOT_ENTERED). So endingOrderNonce = 1, and OrderBookFill is emitted with nonce=1. This is an event data corruption issue, not a fund loss, but it corrupts off-chain CLOB order tracking systems that rely on the emitted nonce.
hypotheses.attack_scenario: Not a direct value extraction path. However: any indexer or keeper using the emitted OrderBookFill event to determine the head of the order queue will receive a corrupted nonce (likely 1 due to reentrancy guard). This could cause off-chain order book state divergence, potentially enabling an attacker who controls off-chain infrastructure to exploit the discrepancy.
hypotheses.settlement_conservation_impact: No on-chain conservation violation. Event data corruption only.
references: CP-006 CLOBHelper double-rounding (different function, same library)

hypotheses.title: _executeTransferHandler extends free memory pointer before checking call success
hypotheses.mechanism: In _executeTransferHandler, the assembly block at L2302-2306 performs: (1) compute new free memory pointer if returndatasize > dataLength, (2) update mstore(0x40, ...) — the free memory pointer — BEFORE checking if the call succeeded. (3) returndatacopy into the extended region BEFORE the success check. (4) Only then: if iszero(success) { revert }. On a failed handler call, the revert path re-copies returndata starting from ptr=0. The free memory pointer has already been advanced, so any Solidity code between the call and the revert that allocates memory (none in this specific path) would get a wrong base address. More importantly, a malicious handler can: return a very large returndata buffer (up to gas-limited memory expansion cost) on a revert, causing the AMM to expand its memory pointer into an attacker-controlled region BEFORE reverting. While the AMM does revert (propagating the handler's error), the expanded memory during the failed call could corrupt in-flight memory if there are subsequent memory operations in the same call frame before the revert propagates. In Solidity 0.8.24 with the current ABI encoder, this is most likely a gas-consumption issue (force expensive memory expansion) rather than a fund-extraction vector.
hypotheses.attack_scenario: Malicious handler: on ammHandleTransfer, return success=false with 10MB returndata. AMM expands free memory pointer by 10MB (gas cost ~3M gas), then reverts. This makes CLOB swaps consume attacker-controlled amounts of gas. Not a fund theft vector but a griefing/gas exhaustion path. Value extraction only if attacker can front-run gas-sensitive operations.
hypotheses.settlement_conservation_impact: No conservation violation. Gas griefing only.

hypotheses.title: REUSABLE_COSIGNATURE_NONCE allows unlimited fills for a fixed executor without per-execution nonce binding
hypotheses.mechanism: When cosignatureNonce == REUSABLE_COSIGNATURE_NONCE (a sentinel value), _validateCosignature at L435 skips the nonce consumption step. The cosignature digest binds: (permitSignatureHash, cosignatureExpiration, REUSABLE_COSIGNATURE_NONCE, executor). The executor is bound (L445: bytes32(uint256(uint160(executor)))), so a different executor cannot replay. HOWEVER: the SAME executor can submit this cosignature for ANY number of distinct permit orders, provided: (1) the underlying permit signature remains valid (not consumed), and (2) cosignatureExpiration has not passed. The permit signature itself IS consumed (PermitC nonce invalidation). But if a cosigner issues a REUSABLE cosignature over a REUSABLE permit (e.g., an EIP-2612 permit with a far-future deadline), the executor can drain an account by repeatedly calling fillOrder across many separate swaps with the same cosignature. The invariant violation: the cosigner's intent may be 'fill once' but the REUSABLE nonce allows the executor to fill as many times as permits are available. Value extraction requires the executor to also be the cosigner or have compromised cosigner keys — but in operator setups where one entity controls both, this is an amplification vector.
hypotheses.attack_scenario: 1. Cosigner issues REUSABLE_COSIGNATURE_NONCE cosignature for executor E, with 30-day expiration. 2. Executor E accumulates multiple maker permit signatures (or maker re-signs permits). 3. Executor E uses the single cosignature to fill ALL those permits within the 30-day window. 4. Cosigner intended to authorize one fill session; executor extracts value across many sessions. Value scales with number of reusable permits and cosignature expiration window.
hypotheses.settlement_conservation_impact: No per-swap conservation violation (each individual fill is correct). Systemic: the cosignature authorization scope is wider than the cosigner likely intended.
references: FP-SUB08 (feeOnTop not signed — REJECTED, different issue)

hypotheses.title: Double WETH↔ETH conversion creates WETH.deposit() liveness dependency for CLOB WETH-tokenOut swaps
hypotheses.mechanism: For CLOB swaps where tokenOut = WETH (Wrapped Native): (1) AMMModule sends ETH to CLOBTransferHandler at L2237 via wrappedNative.withdrawToAccount(recipient=CLOBTransferHandler, amountOut). (2) CLOBTransferHandler.receive() fires (L71), re-wrapping the received ETH back to WETH via WETH.deposit{value: msg.value}(). (3) CLOBTransferHandler now holds WETH. (4) afterSwapRefund at L322 calls WETH.withdrawToAccount(executor, refundAmount), sending ETH to the executor. The double conversion chain (WETH→ETH→WETH→ETH) introduces two WETH.deposit() calls. If at any point the WETH contract has reduced its `receive()` gas stipend or if CLOBTransferHandler's receive() fails (e.g., gas limit edge case in the re-entrancy during deposit), the entire swap reverts. More critically: the receive() at L71 checks `if (msg.sender != WRAPPED_NATIVE)` — but WETH.withdrawToAccount sends ETH from WETH's own balance, making msg.sender = WETH contract. This check passes. However, anyone who directly sends ETH to CLOBTransferHandler (not from WETH contract) causes the check to fail and the transaction reverts. This is protective but means that if the WETH contract address changes (e.g., upgrade) or if a different WETH implementation is used, the receive() guard breaks all CLOB WETH swaps.
hypotheses.attack_scenario: Scenario A (liveness): If WETH.deposit() reverts for any reason (gas exhaustion, WETH upgrade), all CLOB WETH-tokenOut swaps are permanently bricked. Scenario B (fund lock): If CLOBTransferHandler accumulates WETH via the re-wrap mechanism but afterSwapRefund fails silently (it does NOT fail silently — _executeTransferHandlerCallback propagates), WETH could be stuck. More realistic: if WETH.withdrawToAccount is not implemented in a WETH version, the try/catch at L322 falls through to safeTransfer(WETH, executor), which sends WETH tokens instead of ETH — potentially breaking executor expectations.
hypotheses.settlement_conservation_impact: The try/catch at L322 (afterSwapRefund) means: if WETH.withdrawToAccount reverts, the handler falls through and sends WETH tokens directly to the executor instead of ETH. This changes the asset type delivered to the executor — a conservation asymmetry where executor receives WETH instead of ETH. Conservation in token terms is maintained but executor's ETH balance does not increase as expected.

hypotheses.title: Transient tokenOut insolvency window: maker credits accumulate before CLOBTransferHandler receives amountOut
hypotheses.mechanism: Within ammHandleTransfer (CLOBTransferHandler), CLOBHelper.fillOrder at L234 credits makerTokenBalance[maker] += stepOutput for each order filled. These credits represent tokenOut that makers are owed. HOWEVER, at the time fillOrder runs, CLOBTransferHandler has NOT yet received the amountOut from the AMM — that transfer happens AFTER ammHandleTransfer returns (AMMModule L2239: safeTransfer after handler call at L2193). Between L234 (credits accumulate) and L2239 (actual token receipt), there is a transient insolvency: sum(makerTokenBalance) > CLOBTransferHandler.balanceOf(tokenOut). The nonReentrant on ammHandleTransfer (L229) prevents any other call from entering during this window. But the window exists in theory and would be exploitable if nonReentrant could be bypassed (e.g., via a future modifier removal). Currently PROTECTED by nonReentrant, but the design is fragile: if a future version removes nonReentrant from ammHandleTransfer for gas savings, this becomes a critical solvency bug.
hypotheses.attack_scenario: With nonReentrant bypass: 1. During fillOrder execution (while makerTokenBalance credits accumulate but before tokenOut arrives), a reentrant call to withdrawToken would find sum(credits) > balance, effectively withdrawing more than was deposited. Currently infeasible due to nonReentrant. Design note: this is a latent invariant violation.
hypotheses.settlement_conservation_impact: Currently: conservation maintained by nonReentrant ordering. Latent: if nonReentrant is removed, sum(makerTokenBalance) can exceed actual token balance during fillOrder, enabling overdraft via withdrawToken.

hypotheses.title: Price-level resurrection sandwich: openOrder during afterSwapRefund callback resets exhausted CLOB currentPrice
hypotheses.mechanism: CLOBHelper.openOrder (L118-120) updates the order book's currentPrice if the new order price is below the existing currentPrice: `if (sqrtPriceX96 < currentPrice) { ptrOrderBook.currentPrice = sqrtPriceX96; }`. After a swap exhausts the order book, traverseCLOB advances currentPrice to the next price level (potentially type(uint160).max if book is empty). At this point, afterSwapRefund fires (no nonReentrant). If the executor's receive() calls CLOBTransferHandler.openOrder() with a price P_new < current exhausted price, openOrder successfully inserts a new order AND resets currentPrice to P_new. The order book now shows active orders at P_new. A subsequent swap in the same block would fill these orders at P_new, which may be far below fair market value — a classic front-running/sandwich setup. The attacker profits: buy at P_low before the victim swap, victim's swap exhausts book, attacker's ETH callback inserts new order at P_low, attacker captures fills at P_low from the next victim.
hypotheses.attack_scenario: 1. Block N: Attacker calls openOrder at P_low with tokenIn. 2. Block N: Victim submits swap that fills through P_low and beyond, exhausting attacker's order. Attacker profits from victim fill. 3. afterSwapRefund ETH callback fires → attacker's receive() calls openOrder(P_low) again instantly. 4. Block N+1: Another victim's swap hits P_low again — attacker captures two rounds of fill profit with a single initial deposit of capital. Net effect: attacker amplifies returns by recycling capital within the swap callback window.
hypotheses.settlement_conservation_impact: Per-swap conservation: maintained (each fill is correct per current book state). Inter-swap: attacker captures outsized value from price level resurrection that happens outside normal market mechanics.

hypotheses.title: CP-006 extraction vector: calculateFixedInput double-rounding systematically over-credits makers at taker (executor) expense in fillOrder
hypotheses.mechanism:
calculateFixedInput applies FullMath.mulDivRoundingUp TWICE (L313 then L314). Each call independently rounds up, inflating amountOut by up to 1 wei each, for a combined over-rounding of up to 2 wei per invocation. In fillOrder(), at each step: stepOutput = calculateFixedInput(stepInput, currentPrice) is credited to makerTokenBalance[maker] (L234) and subtracted from fillOutputRemaining (L232). The executor (taker) receives fillOutputRemaining as a refund via afterSwapRefund. Because each step over-rounds by up to 2 wei, the sum of step credits exceeds the exact price, meaning fillOutputRemaining is correspondingly reduced. Over a fill spanning N order steps, the executor loses up to 2N wei of tokenOut to the systematic over-crediting of makers. This is confirmed by the CP-006 finding classification.

Attacker-controlled amplification: a maker can fragment a large order into many small sub-orders (all at the same price bucket). Each fill step calling calculateFixedInput costs one separate invocation with its own rounding. With 10,000 small orders at one price, a single fill loses up to 20,000 wei (2 × 10,000 steps) relative to the correct price. With 18-decimal ERC20s, this is 20,000 / 1e18 ≈ 2e-14 units — tiny per swap. But repeated many times per block (e.g., 100 swaps × 20,000 wei = 2,000,000 wei = 2e-12 units) the extraction compounds.
hypotheses.attack_scenario: 1. Attacker (maker) opens 10,000 orders of 1 wei each at sqrtPriceX96=P, spending 10,000 wei of tokenIn. 2. A taker submits a swap filling all 10,000 orders. Each step credits maker by true_output + up to 2 wei. 3. Maker withdraws makerTokenBalance — receives up to true_output + 20,000 wei. 4. Executor receives fillOutputRemaining = (outputAmount - sum_of_credited) which is 20,000 wei less than expected. 5. Attacker repeats across many swaps. Gas cost for 10,000 order openings vs 20,000 wei gain must be analyzed.
hypotheses.settlement_conservation_impact: Conservation within the CLOB is maintained (sum credits + fillOutputRemaining == outputAmount). The loss is to the TAKER (executor), not to the CLOB's own reserves. This is a wealth transfer from takers to makers when a swap spans many fill steps.
references: CP-006 (CONFIRMED Medium — this hypothesis adds the specific extraction amplification vector via order fragmentation)

hypotheses.title: feeOnTop siphons positive slippage from partial fill permit swaps — executor extracts unsigned fee between limitAmount and true market price
hypotheses.mechanism:
The SWAP_TYPEHASH_STUB (Constants.sol L35-38) defines: 'Swap(bool partialFill,address recipient,int256 amountSpecified,uint256 limitAmount,address tokenOut,address exchangeFeeRecipient,uint16 exchangeFeeBPS,address cosigner,address hook)'. The feeOnTop fields (recipient + flatAmount or BPS) are ABSENT. Both _executeFillOrKillPermit (lines 226-239) and _executePartialFillPermit (lines 345-357) compute additionalDataHash WITHOUT feeOnTop. This means the user's EIP-712 signature does not bind feeOnTop; the executor can set it to any value at execution time.

In AMMModule lines 2225-2232, feeOnTopAmount is deducted from the tokenIn received from the user and sent to feeOnTop.recipient (executor-controlled). The pool then processes (amountIn - exchangeFee - feeOnTop) of effective tokenIn, returning correspondingly less tokenOut.

For partial fills, the ratio check (lines 319-326) is: amountIn <= mulDiv(permitLimitAmount, amountOut, permitAmountSpecified). With feeOnTop: amountIn is the FULL user-deposited amount but amountOut is REDUCED (because the pool received less effective input). The executor can tune feeOnTop to maximize extraction while keeping: amountOut >= (amountIn * permitAmountSpecified / permitLimitAmount), i.e., keeping the ratio check passing.

Maximum extractable feeOnTop per swap: solve for feeOnTopAmount where:
  amountOut(amountIn - exchangeFee - feeOnTopAmount) >= amountIn * permitAmountSpecified / permitLimitAmount
This allows the executor to pocket up to the positive slippage (true market price - user's signed floor price) as feeOnTop.
hypotheses.attack_scenario: 1. User signs partial fill permit: limitAmount=1000 USDC, amountSpecified=1 ETH. Pool quotes 1.05 ETH for 1000 USDC (5% positive slippage). 2. Executor computes feeOnTop = {recipient: executor, flatAmount: 47 USDC} such that 953 USDC going to pool still returns >= 1 ETH (barely meeting the user's floor). 3. Executor submits swap: user pays 1000 USDC, gets 1 ETH (minimum), executor takes 47 USDC as feeOnTop. 4. The 47 USDC represents the captured positive slippage that the user would otherwise have received as extra ETH.
hypotheses.settlement_conservation_impact: Conservation maintained (tokenIn received = pool input + fees + feeOnTop). But user receives their signed minimum rather than market price — the excess is silently redirected to executor via unsigned feeOnTop.
references: FP-SUB08 (REJECTED) — this hypothesis provides the specific mathematical extraction path (positive slippage capture) that may not have been characterized in the original rejection. Rejection reason: feeOnTop is intentionally controlled by cosigner-authorized executor.

hypotheses.title: Settlement conservation structural gap: no post-callback tokenOut invariant check — AMM trusts handler to conserve tokenOut
hypotheses.mechanism:
AMMModule._finalizeSwapCollectFundsAndDisburse enforces tokenIn conservation via a strict balance check (L2207-2213): balanceInBefore + amountIn == balanceInAfter. There is NO equivalent balance check for tokenOut.

Execution order:
1. L2180: snapshot balanceInBefore
2. L2193-2203: call ammHandleTransfer (handler sends tokenIn to AMM; handler updates internal state)
3. L2207-2213: ENFORCE tokenIn balance invariant ✓
4. L2217-2232: AMM sends exchangeFee + feeOnTop of tokenIn out
5. L2235-2244: AMM sends amountOut of tokenOut to recipient — NO POST-SEND CHECK
6. L2251: AMM executes handler callback (afterSwapRefund) — NO tokenOut balance check after callback

The AMM's only hard conservation invariant is on the INPUT side. The output side relies entirely on:
(a) the pool type computing amountOut correctly, and
(b) the handler's callback not redirecting tokenOut to unintended recipients.

For CLOBTransferHandler, (b) is maintained correctly: afterSwapRefund only sends fillOutputRemaining (= outputAmount - sum_maker_credits ≤ outputAmount). But this is a convention, not enforced by the AMM. Any future handler or handler upgrade that manipulates tokenOut post-delivery has no on-chain invariant blocking it — only the handler's own correctness guarantees conservation.
hypotheses.attack_scenario: Scenario requires a compromised or malicious handler. Handler correctly deposits tokenIn (passing the only enforced check), then encodes callbackData that drains excess tokenOut from the handler's pre-existing balance (accumulated from prior swaps not yet claimed by makers). AMM executes the callback, sending extra tokenOut to attacker-controlled address. AMM sees no violation because there is no tokenOut balance check. This is not exploitable with current CLOBTransferHandler (afterSwapRefund sends only fillOutputRemaining) but represents a systemic design gap for the handler interface.
hypotheses.settlement_conservation_impact: Currently maintained by handler code correctness. The AMM provides no on-chain safety net for tokenOut conservation, creating a one-sided trust model: tokenIn is checked, tokenOut is trusted.

hypotheses.title: _enforceTokenHooks price bound validation uses double-rounded amountOut — orders at configured price boundary may be incorrectly accepted or rejected
hypotheses.mechanism:
_enforceTokenHooks (L590) computes amountOut = CLOBHelper.calculateFixedInput(orderAmount, sqrtPriceX96) and passes it to hook.validateHandlerOrder. This uses the same double-rounded formula as fillOrder (CP-006 root cause), inflating amountOut by up to 2 wei.

AMMStandardHook.validateHandlerOrder (lines 215-223) computes effectiveSqrtPriceX96 = SqrtPriceCalculator.computeRatioX96(amountOut, orderAmount), then checks effectiveSqrtPriceX96 <= maxSqrtPriceX96 (and >= minSqrtPriceX96).

Because amountOut is over-rounded: effectiveSqrtPriceX96 > true sqrtPriceX96 by a small margin. Effect direction:
- Orders near maxSqrtPriceX96 bound: inflated effectiveSqrtPriceX96 may exceed maxSqrtPriceX96, causing valid orders to be REJECTED (false reject)
- Orders near minSqrtPriceX96 bound: inflated effectiveSqrtPriceX96 may push an order that is truly below minSqrtPriceX96 to appear above it, causing invalid orders to be ACCEPTED (false accept → price bound bypass)

The second case (false accept) is the value extraction angle: an attacker places an order at sqrtPriceX96 = minSqrtPriceX96 - epsilon, betting that the over-rounding of calculateFixedInput(orderAmount, minSqrtPriceX96 - epsilon) causes computeRatioX96 to return a value >= minSqrtPriceX96, bypassing the lower bound check.
hypotheses.attack_scenario: 1. Pool configured with minSqrtPriceX96 = P_min. 2. Attacker finds epsilon such that calculateFixedInput(largeAmount, P_min - epsilon) > calculateFixedInput_exact(largeAmount, P_min). 3. computeRatioX96(inflated_amountOut, largeAmount) yields effectiveSqrtPriceX96 >= P_min. 4. Order at P_min - epsilon is accepted by hook. 5. When a taker fills this order, they receive amountIn at P_min - epsilon — below the configured minimum — paying more tokenIn per unit of tokenOut than the pool policy intended.
hypotheses.settlement_conservation_impact: Not a direct fund loss. Enables orders below configured price bounds, potentially allowing fills at prices that violate pool policy. Economic harm depends on how far P_min - epsilon can be from P_min while still bypassing the check (at most 2 wei of amountOut inflation, limiting the bypass to microscopic price deltas).
references: Guardian H-01 (Missing Hook In CLOB — ACKNOWLEDGED)
